title: Testing Frameworks and Migration Tooling
bodyMarkdown:
# Testing Frameworks and Migration Tooling

Architects advise teams on two related questions: **how do we prove a system is ready** before and during deployment, and **which tool moves which workload** during a migration. Both are high-yield on the exam because they reward matching a requirement to a specific tool or test type, and both punish "familiar" answers that do not fit the workload.

## The testing pyramid

Balance test types by speed, cost, and quantity. Google's [DevOps capabilities guidance](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/devops/devops-tech-test-automation) lists test automation (reliable automated suites run throughout the delivery lifecycle) and test data management among the practices that drive delivery performance.

| Layer | Quantity | Speed | What it proves | Typical gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Unit | Many | Seconds | One function or class in isolation, with mocks | Every commit, first Cloud Build step |
| Integration | Some | Seconds to minutes | Components together, such as a service plus its datastore | Pull request or merge, often against local emulators |
| End-to-end / system | Few | Minutes or more | The full deployed stack on critical paths | After deploy, for example a Cloud Deploy verify step |
| Load / stress / soak | Few, scheduled | Long | Non-functional behavior at scale | Pre-launch and before high-traffic events |

The exam trap is the inverted pyramid: end-to-end tests on every commit, or manual QA as the only gate. Unit tests belong at the base because they give the fastest regression feedback.

Tests connect to the delivery pipeline at specific points. Unit and static checks run as Cloud Build steps. Post-deploy checks run in Cloud Deploy, which [runs your verification containers](https://cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/verify-deployment) after a deployment and treats exit code 0 as success; a non-zero exit fails the verification and therefore the rollout. A [canary phase](https://cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/deployment-strategies/canary) can add deploy analysis using Google Cloud Observability metrics so metrics, not people, decide whether to advance.

### Testing infrastructure code

Infrastructure code tests behave differently from application tests. Google's [Terraform testing guidance](https://cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/best-practices/testing) says a real test creates, modifies, and destroys real infrastructure, so it is slow and costs money, and you cannot purely unit test an end-to-end architecture. The recommended order, in ascending cost and depth, is:

1. **Static analysis**, such as `terraform validate`, linters, and dry runs.
2. **Module integration tests**, deploying one module into a test environment (frameworks include Google's blueprint testing framework, Terratest, Kitchen-Terraform, InSpec, and tftest).
3. **End-to-end tests**, deploying all modules into a fresh environment that resembles production.

Practices from the same page: break the architecture into modules and test them individually; avoid reusing state between tests; randomize project IDs and resource names; test in an isolated environment (ideally a fresh project or folder per test, with a service account per run); and clean up everything.

## Load, stress, and soak testing

These validate non-functional requirements and are the correct answer when the scenario says "sustain 10x traffic," "find the breaking point," or "degradation over time."

- **Load test**: expected and multiples of expected concurrency, measured against latency and error-rate targets.
- **Stress test**: push past limits to find the breaking point and see how the system fails (gracefully, or by cascading).
- **Spike test**: a sudden jump in traffic to check how quickly autoscaling and caches respond.
- **Soak (endurance) test**: sustained load for hours to expose memory leaks, connection exhaustion, and slow degradation.

Open-source tools such as **Locust**, **k6**, and **Apache JMeter** generate concurrent virtual users. Practical rules: generate load from infrastructure you control and can scale (for example a GKE job or a fleet of VMs) rather than a laptop; use a production-like environment and data volume; watch Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging during the run so you see saturation before users would; and never point a stress test at a shared production system without a plan to stop it. Unit tests, static analysis, and a single end-to-end request do not answer capacity questions.

## Migration: framing before tools

Google's [migration guide](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/migration-to-gcp-getting-started) describes four phases: **Assess** (inventory, dependencies, TCO, performance baselines), **Plan** (identity, resource hierarchy, networking, prioritized strategy), **Deploy** (execute the migration and move data), and **Optimize**. It defines six migration types:

| Type | Meaning | Illustrative tooling |
|---|---|---|
| Rehost | Lift and shift with minimal change | Migrate to Virtual Machines |
| Replatform | Lift and optimize | Database Migration Service, Migrate to Containers |
| Refactor | Move and improve | Code changes, then deploy to Cloud Run or GKE |
| Re-architect | Continue to modernize | Redesign, often to microservices |
| Rebuild | Remove and replace (rip and replace) | New build |
| Repurchase | Move to a different product, often SaaS | Vendor tooling |

(Some sources use a seven-R list that adds retire and retain; Google's own guide enumerates the six above, so answer from that list.)

## Migration tooling decision guide

| Workload | Tool |
|---|---|
| VMware, AWS, or Azure VMs to Compute Engine | **Migrate to Virtual Machines** |
| Databases into Cloud SQL or AlloyDB | **Database Migration Service (DMS)** |
| Object and file data into Cloud Storage over the network (more than about 1 TB) | **Storage Transfer Service** |
| Large or poorly connected data, offline | **Transfer Appliance** |
| Scheduled loads into BigQuery from SaaS, warehouses, or other clouds | **BigQuery Data Transfer Service** |
| VM-hosted applications to containers on GKE or Cloud Run | **Migrate to Containers** |
| Under 1 TB, ad hoc | `gcloud storage` |

### Migrate to Virtual Machines

[Migrate to Virtual Machines](https://cloud.google.com/migrate/virtual-machines/docs/5.0/concepts/lifecycle) lifts and shifts VMs from vSphere, AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud VMware Engine to Compute Engine. It continuously replicates disk data without downtime on the source, then you create **test clones** from the replicated data, and finally perform a predictable **cut-over**. The phases are onboard, replicate, set target details, test-clone, cut-over, and finalize. After the first full replication, incremental replication runs every two hours by default using Change Block Tracking. **OS adaptations** are applied after each replication step (network configuration, the Compute Engine agent, serial console). Cut-over stops the source VM, finalizes replication, and creates the production instance; it includes a short downtime and belongs in a maintenance window, only after test-clone validation. It is for whole VMs, not for databases or files.

### Database Migration Service

[DMS](https://cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/overview) migrates databases into **Cloud SQL and AlloyDB for PostgreSQL**. It manages networking, the initial snapshot, and ongoing replication. Know the vocabulary: **continuous** (online) migration follows an initial dump and load with change data capture, so you cut over when source and destination are in sync for minimal downtime; **one-time** migration is a snapshot, so applications with writes face downtime. **Homogeneous** means the same engine (MySQL to Cloud SQL for MySQL); **heterogeneous** means different engines (Oracle to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL), where DMS offers Gemini-powered conversion features.

### Storage Transfer Service and Transfer Appliance

[Storage Transfer Service](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/docs/overview) moves data between Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, Cloud Storage, on-premises file systems, HDFS, and public URLs, with TLS 1.3 and integrity validation. It is optimized for transfers over 1 TiB, can run Google-managed or with self-hosted agents, and carries no SLA. Google's [transfer options](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/docs/transfer-options) say: from another cloud, use Storage Transfer Service; under 1 TB from on-premises or between Cloud Storage regions, use `gcloud storage`; over 1 TB from on-premises, Storage Transfer Service or Transfer Appliance; and with poor or no connectivity, Transfer Appliance. [Transfer Appliance](https://cloud.google.com/transfer-appliance/docs/4.0/overview) is a ruggedized, tamper-evident device you fill, ship to a Google upload facility, and Google uploads to your bucket; data is AES-256 encrypted with keys you can manage in Cloud KMS, and the device is wiped to NIST 800-88.

### BigQuery Data Transfer Service and Migrate to Containers

The [BigQuery Data Transfer Service](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/dts-introduction) automates scheduled, managed loads into BigQuery from sources including Salesforce, Amazon Redshift, Teradata, Snowflake, Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Ads, and others, with backfills to recover gaps. It cannot transfer data out of BigQuery. [Migrate to Containers](https://cloud.google.com/migrate/containers/docs/getting-started) modernizes VM-based applications (WebSphere, JBoss, Apache, Tomcat, WordPress, Windows IIS, and Linux-based apps) into containers for GKE, GKE Autopilot, or Cloud Run.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Using the wrong tool for the data type.** Storage Transfer Service moves objects, not live databases; DMS moves databases, not files; Migrate to Virtual Machines moves VMs, not BigQuery tables.
- **Migrating a live database with a one-time snapshot** when the requirement says minimal downtime; choose continuous replication.
- **Cutting over without a test clone.** The test-clone phase exists to validate before the short cutover downtime.
- **Copying hundreds of terabytes through a script or bastion host** instead of Storage Transfer Service or Transfer Appliance.
- **Treating load testing as a per-commit task** or running it only after launch; it is a pre-launch gate for known traffic events.
- **Inverted test pyramid** with mostly slow end-to-end tests.
- **Reusing state or shared projects between infrastructure tests**, which causes name collisions and accidental deletions.
- **Skipping Assess.** Migrating before dependency discovery and baselines turns cutovers into outages.

## Exam tips

- **VMs lift-and-shift: Migrate to Virtual Machines.** Look for "VMware, AWS, or Azure VMs, minimal downtime, test before cutover" and choose test clones plus a scheduled cut-over.
- **Databases: DMS with continuous replication.** "Minimal downtime" means continuous migration with change data capture; "one-time" means downtime.
- **Files and objects: Storage Transfer Service, or Transfer Appliance if offline.** Over 1 TB across a network is Storage Transfer Service; poor connectivity is Transfer Appliance; under 1 TB is `gcloud storage`.
- **BigQuery loads on a schedule: BigQuery Data Transfer Service.** It loads data in; it is not a general copy tool and cannot export.
- **Unit tests are the base of the pyramid.** Fastest feedback, run on every commit; end-to-end tests are few.
- **"Sustain 10x traffic and find the breaking point" is load plus stress testing** with Locust, k6, or JMeter, not unit, static, or single-path integration tests.
- **Tool by workload type, not familiarity.** Match the noun (VM, database, object store, warehouse) to the tool.
- **Google lists six migration types.** Rehost, replatform, refactor, re-architect, rebuild, repurchase; rehost pairs with Migrate to Virtual Machines.
